rounds.response:
Maya — a quick rule: the variable with more probability mass on values far from its center is more spread out, so scan for heavier tails or extremes (you can also compare E[X^2] quickly instead of doing the full Var formula).  
Jared — most course platforms lock submissions at the deadline, but instructors/TA can sometimes allow a replacement if you contact them immediately and explain the issue.  
Linh — yes, dividing each p by the total 0.9 is correct here (p_i' = p_i/0.9) and is appropriate when the list is meant to be a probability distribution but was scaled or rounded; don’t renormalize if the extra/missing mass represents real missing outcomes or data errors you shouldn’t hide.  
Omar — for Y = −1,0,1 you can check directly: P(|Y−0.1| ≤ 1) = P(Y=0 or 1) = 0.5+0.3 = 0.8, so 80% is within 1 unit; more generally Chebyshev’s inequality gives a conservative bound (≥51% within 1 unit here).  
Sara — yes: P(X ≥ 2) = sum of the probabilities of all values 2 and above (or compute 1 − P(X ≤ 1) as a shortcut).
